Oh, yeah, yeah, right up here. The 10,200th meeting of the Security Council is resumed. I wish to remind all speakers to limit their statements to no more than 3 minutes in order to enable the Council to carry out its work expeditiously. The flashing light on the microphone will prompt speakers to bring their remarks to a close after 3 minutes. I now give the floor to the representative of Ukraine.

Thank you, Mr. President. I thank the Democratic Republic of Congo presidency for organizing today's important debate. We also thank the briefers for their valuable contribution. It was rightly mentioned today that natural resources can either fuel conflict or become a foundation for peace and prosperity. Unfortunately, Ukraine's experience clearly demonstrates how an aggressor state can exploit natural resources to finance war, undermine sovereignty, and threaten international peace and security. And Russia is doing exactly that. It transformed Ukraine's natural resources from assets of development into the instruments of war. Even today, the Russian representative attempted to blame others in starting wars to invade foreign territories and exploit resource. But he missed the beam in his own eye. Russia, as an aggressor state, doesn't have legal and moral right in this Council to discuss and interfere with our sovereign right to use our resources. Since the beginning of its full-scale invasion, Russia has systematically seized, illegally appropriated, and exploited Ukraine's natural resources. And it's about coal, iron ore, critical minerals, agricultural land, forests, water resources, and other national assets. Russia is stealing our wheat and oilseeds and other produce. Such actions violate international law. It deprives Ukraine of its sovereign resources and provides additional revenues to sustain Russia's war and prolong its aggression against Ukraine. Mr. President, this also demonstrates that the challenge before us is a broader issue. Thus, the international community must also address the illegal extraction, trade, and export of natural resources originating from occupied territories and ensure that such resources never enter legitimate international markets. And we thank our partners for imposing robust sanctions regimes against Russia. Strengthening transparency and traceability throughout the global supply chains is therefore essential. States and business alike must ensure that resources illegally extracted from occupied territories are neither imported nor traded. And we don't have to shy away here in the Council from bringing into accountability those who help Russia to exploit our natural resources. Mr. President, Ukraine believes that natural resources governance cannot be separated from respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of states. Sustainability management of natural resources is impossible where international law is violated, territories are occupied, and local communities are deprived of their own rights. As the world moves towards the green and digital transition, demand for critical raw materials will continue to grow. That makes it even more important to ensure that resources become drivers of sustainable development, but not the instruments of coercion or aggression. We therefore support efforts to strengthen international cooperation, improve traceability mechanisms, promote transparency and accountability, and prevent the illicit exploitation of natural resources. Mr. President, natural resources must never become a reward for aggression, or a source of financing wars. Every nation holds the foundational right to use its natural resources to pursue national development, prosperity and well-being, but it should be supported by robust implementation of UN Charter and international law. Once a renowned Indian agronomist, Dr. Samintahan, said, and I quote, the future belongs to nations who have grains but not guns. Guns you can purchase, grains you cannot. So the future is not about wars, but about our cooperation together on the peaceful use of scarce resources. I thank you, Mr. President.
I would like to thank the representative of Ukraine for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Germany.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, we would like to thank the Democratic Republic of the Congo for convening today's timely debate. We believe this is an important debate because it rightly shifts the focus on how responsible resource governance can actually prevent conflicts and contribute to development, peace, and prosperity. In this context, we would like to make 3 short points. First, we believe that natural resource governance can only be successful if it anticipates future security risks. And we further believe that this discussion should go beyond minerals and include critical resources such as fertile land and water. Second, we cannot ignore central risk multipliers such as environmental degradation and climate change. Their impact on fragile contexts is increasing, a fact which any successful natural resource governance and conflict prevention, for that matter, must address in a more systematic manner. Germany aims at integrating these findings in its own action. We have therefore increased investments in environmental peacebuilding, for instance by contributing over €20 million since 2022 to the Weathering Risk Initiative for programs in the Bay of Bengal, Iraq, Yemen, Somalia, and Nigeria. It is also an increasingly important component of our bilateral partnerships. Germany and Mozambique, for example, cooperate on strengthening environmental oversight on the mining sector. Recently, a major milestone has been reached in Nigeria. Over the past 20 years, the Nigerian state of Benue has been severely affected by climate-accelerated resource conflicts. Supported by Germany, the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue has facilitated a peace process in Benue State, which led to the signing of a statewide landmark natural resource peace agreement just June 29th of this month—

of this year.

The agreement, developed with the active participation of marginalized groups, recognizes the impact of climate change as a driver of conflict and contains specific provisions for the peaceful management of natural resources. Third and finally, the issue, we believe, cannot be solved by the affected countries alone. We must look at the bigger picture, and we especially have to look at global supply chains. Responsible supply chains are an investment in peace and security. Producing, transit, and consumer countries all share responsibility for ensuring that mineral wealth benefits producing states and local communities rather than financing armed groups. This requires effective due diligence, responsible investments, and greater local value creation. Germany supports this approach, for example, in the DRC through the Sustainable Resource Supply Chain Program, which specifically promotes the formalization of the artisanal mining sector. President, in conclusion, I want to assure you that Germany remains committed to our common objective: natural resources must contribute to prosperity and peace and not to conflict. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Germany for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of India.

Mr. President, we thank the Democratic Republic of Congo for convening this timely debate. India recognizes that the illicit exploitation and trafficking of natural resources can, in certain situations, contribute to the financing of armed groups and prolonged conflict. However, we must remember that natural resources are first and foremost an engine of development and prosperity for sovereign states. The challenge before us is therefore not the existence of natural resources themselves, but ensuring that they are governed in a transparent, accountable, and nationally owned manner for the benefit of present and future generations. The primary responsibility for the governance and management of natural resources rests with sovereign states. National ownership, capacity building, and institution strengthening should therefore remain at the centre of all national and international efforts, solutions must be tailored to national circumstances and implemented with the full consent and leadership of the countries concerned. At the same time, it's a responsibility of states to ensure that subnational provinces that are rich in resources like oil and gas, minerals, rare earths, and precious metals, and provide the basis of sustenance for local communities, have an equitable and just share in the benefits derived from these resources in order to avoid internal instability and insecurity, not just within such countries but also in the wider region. The consequences of not doing so are clearly visible, including in our own region. Mr. President, provinces that are resource-rich but development-poor become centers of insecurity that radiate instability beyond their borders, even into neighboring countries. Further, this instability also attracts transborder interventions and resource extraction by external actors, which further exacerbates grievances of local communities and fuels instability. A heavy-handed and securitized approach to governance of resource-rich provinces only makes matters worse. India believes that responsible supply chains, greater transparency, good governance, and enhanced due diligence can contribute to reducing opportunities for illicit trade while enabling producing countries and subnational regions to derive greater developmental benefits from their natural wealth. Equally important is promoting local value addition, technology partnerships, and investment that help resource-rich developing countries move beyond being exporters of raw materials and become active participants across global value chains. Mr. President, while discussing these important issues, it's equally essential to preserve the respective mandates of the principal organs of the United Nations and also of other UN institutions. The Security Council has a clearly defined responsibility under the Charter for the maintenance of international peace and security. Broader questions relating to sustainable development, natural resource governance, climate action, and economic cooperation appropriately belong within the mandates of the General Assembly, the ECOSOC, the UNDP, the UNFCCC, etc. Maintaining this institutional balance is critical to ensuring both effectiveness and legitimacy within the multilateral system. The Peacebuilding Commission in particular can make a valuable contribution given its inclusive composition by supporting nationally owned efforts to strengthen institutions, enhance transparent and accountable natural resource governance, mobilize international support for capacity building, and foster inclusive dialogue among governments, local communities, and development partners. Its comparative advantage lies in bringing together diverse stakeholders dealing with peace, with development and financing in support of nationally identified priorities while fully respecting the sovereignty of the countries concerned. India therefore supports strengthening international cooperation to combat the illicit exploitation of natural resources, promote responsible and resilient supply chains, and assist countries in building governance capacities where requested. While fully respecting the purposes and principles of the Charter of the UN, Our collective objective should be to enable natural resources to become drivers of sustainable development, shared prosperity, and lasting peace so that no one is left behind. Mr. President, it was not our intention to bring other issues in this forum, but my delegation is compelled to respond to Pakistan as it has chosen to misuse today's discussion to peddle its false narrative. Our position on the Indus Water Treaty remains clear and consistent. Cooperation on the basis of mutual trust and goodwill cannot be expected when cross-border terrorism is regularly deployed as an instrument of state policy. As for the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, it has always been, is, and will remain an integral and inalienable part of India. This is a constitutional and legal reality that Pakistan deliberately chooses to ignore. The only outstanding issue with regard to Jammu and Kashmir is a naked aggression and illegal occupation of India's sovereign territory by Pakistan. Instead of pointing fingers at India, Pakistan would serve itself and its people far better by putting its own house in order. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of India for the statement, and I give the floor to the representative of Egypt.

Mr. President, we would like to thank the Democratic Republic of the Congo for convening this important meeting, which addresses an issue that lies at the very heart of the nexus between peace and security and sustainable development. Egypt affirms that natural resources are not in and of themselves a cause of conflict. Rather, it is their poor governance, illicit exploitation, the absence of equity and transparency in the distribution of their revenues, and external interference aimed at appropriating them that transform them from a source of development and prosperity into a driver of conflict terrorism and organized crime. Conversely, sound national governance, enhanced transparency, local value addition, and ensuring that communities benefit from resource revenues can transform such natural resources into pillars of stability and peacebuilding. This is fully consistent with the objective of this debate: to move from the resource curse to the resource blessing whereby natural wealth contributes to financing peace and development instead of fueling wars and conflicts and draining the capacities of states and peoples to advance and prosper. Thus, Egypt underscores the need to address the gaps that enable networks engaged in the illicit exploitation of natural resources. Efforts should not be limited to the sites of resource extraction, as was stated by the Secretary General this morning. Instead, they should target those who transport, smuggle, purchase, and integrate such resources into international supply chains and markets. It's equally essential to strengthen accountability mechanisms and frameworks for all actors benefiting from such activities, while fully respecting the sovereignty of states and their permanent sovereignty over their natural resources. Mr. President, Egypt expresses its full solidarity with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. We reaffirm their sovereign right to exercise control over their natural resources and their utilization for the benefit of their people, free from illicit exploitation or external interference. The DRC's vast mineral wealth should no longer serve as a driver of continued conflict in the eastern part of the country or as a source of profit for armed groups and other criminal mining and smuggling networks. Rather, it should become a catalyst for industrial development, value-added production, and other complementary economic and development activities that create employment opportunities and improve the lives of local communities. In this regard, Egypt emphasizes the importance of supporting the Congolese national capacities in the areas of natural resource management, supply chain tracking and monitoring, combating smuggling corruption and border management. It also highlights the importance of supporting disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration programs, security sector reform, and strengthening state authority and law enforcement institutions in resource-rich areas. From this Security Council, Egypt also calls for supporting the DRC in transitioning from the export of raw materials to domestic manufacturing and value addition inside the country, thereby ensuring that the Congolese people receive a fair share of their wealth. The concept of natural resources, Mr. President, is not confined to minerals and energy sources, as was stated by my colleague from Germany a while ago. Water, particularly the waters of transboundary rivers, is among the resources most closely linked to the survival of peoples and to their food, economic, and social security.
Thank you.

Against this backdrop, Egypt affirms that the management of international rivers must be based on cooperation, good faith, equitable and reasonable utilization, and the obligation not to cause significant harm, as well as prior notification and consultation regarding projects that may have transboundary impacts. We further emphasize the importance of reaching balanced and legally binding agreements that take into account the rights and interests of all riparian states, while rejecting the imposition of fait accompli or unilateral measures that could undermine the water security of peoples or threaten their stability and development. Mr. President, Egypt would like to propose the following recommendations. First, to develop an integrated U.N. approach linking natural resource governance with conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and development, while respecting national jurisdiction and the full national ownership of natural resources. Second, to strengthen traceability and transparency mechanisms for mineral supply chains and reinforce the relevant policy and criminal justice frameworks to ensure accountability for parties, companies, and intermediaries involved in the illicit trade in the natural resources of conflict-affected states. Third, to direct international support towards strengthening and building national institutions, enhancing border management, combatting corruption and developing domestic industries and value chains, thereby ensuring that producing countries and local communities benefit from the revenues generated by their natural resources. Fourth, to integrate transboundary water resources into conflict prevention efforts and encourage riparian states and river basin countries to reach legally binding agreements through good faith negotiations and in accordance with international law, while refraining from unilateral measures that may cause harm to co-repairing states or threaten regional peace and security. Fifth and last, to strengthen cooperation between the UN, the African Union, and regional organizations while supporting African initiatives aimed at transforming natural resources into a driver of development, integration, reconstruction, and peacebuilding. Mr. President, in conclusion, Egypt reaffirms that achieving sustainable Peace requires that natural wealth should never become a source of suffering for peoples, but rather an instrument for their empowerment and for realizing their legitimate aspirations for development, prosperity, and stability. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Egypt for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Morocco.

Mr. President, at the outset, I would like to applaud the sisterly Democratic Republic of the Congo. Thank you for convening this very timely, pressing debate. Ms. Thérèse Kayekwamba Wagner, Minister for Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Francophonie, we would like to extend our respect to you. We very much appreciated Thank you very much, Mr. President, for your briefing. And we very much like the fact that we're discussing a cause that is of interest to all nations, entire continents. We would also like to express our gratitude to the Secretary-General and to the Director-General of the World Trade Organization. Thank you for your briefings. Mr. President, natural resource governance is one of the issues which affects the future of international peace and security the most. It addresses and touches upon conflict prevention, interstate relations, sustainable development, and therefore this topic deserves the unswerving attention of the Security Council. We are debating not the resources themselves, but rather the governance thereof. The energy transition will be accelerating by the year 2030, and there are already regions which are very vulnerable, which will be even harder hit. And this is something UN programs, especially the Environment Program, is documenting. There is the illicit exploitation of a number of these resources, and that's fueling instability in a number of the world's regions instead of contributing to development. The resource curse is first and foremost a product of a deficit in governance, traceability, and cooperation. The Security Council has unstintingly looked at this issue with sanctions regimes and panels of experts. We've supported the Kimberley Process, but all of these instruments, although they're very useful, would be better placed if they were part and parcel of a more coherent, integrated approach. Which anticipates crises before they break out. Mr. President, we remain convinced that responsible resource governance is a vector of stability and development. It is in this spirit that my delegation would like to underscore the 3 following points. First, minerals traceability, which deprives armed groups from sources of funding and allows us to ensure, through tailored certification mechanisms, that minerals supply does not feed into violence. That's key. Second, building national capacity for controlling resources would allow all member states to reap the benefits of its own resources and to channel them to the development of their nation, of their people. Third, environmental and climatic governance should be part of prevention strategies because as resources become more scarce, a process exacerbated by climate change, Thank you. It calls for proactive rather than reactive governance. Mr. President, this vision— the Kingdom of Morocco will not simply speak about it. We want to translate these words into deeds. In July, all member states of the Economic Community for West Africa, including a number of other states as well, agreed on infrastructure that will be linking 13 countries in the region to— we agreed to share energy resources, creating a corridor of development, regional integration, and prosperity. Together with good governance mechanisms, this should result in $27 billion in economic benefits. This project illustrates that well-governed resources can become locomotives for regional prosperity and development. On top of this commitment, there is also the initiative of His Majesty the King An Atlantic initiative to address enclaves in the Sahel, landlocked countries in the Sahel, and we aim to do this through regional integration. All of these initiatives follow a similar logic: geography, national resources, natural resources, as well as African solidarity and cooperation. All of the above can be drivers of stability and shared prosperity at the continental level. Now, moving beyond the continent, this conviction also fuels our international partnerships. In fact, in February of this year, we signed a framework agreement with the United States on critical minerals, the objective being to bolster resilience, supply chain diversification at the global level. This is a clear demonstration of what trust-based cooperation, transparency-based partnerships can By way of conclusion, the Kingdom of Morocco very much hopes that this debate will serve as a step towards better good resource governance in the interests of peace, stability, and shared development. I thank you for your kind attention.
I thank the representative of Morocco for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of South Africa.

Thank you very much for giving me the floor, Mr. President. My delegation would like to commend the DRC's presidency for convening this open debate and the priority that it places on the issue of natural resource governance. Mr. President, in the context of the uncertain geopolitical climate where supply chains of critical minerals are threatened, we have to focus on the role of natural resources specifically on critical minerals, which holds immense potential in a just energy transition and technological advancement, in fueling conflict in various parts of the world. Certification processes and due diligence frameworks such as the Kimberley Process, the regional certification mechanism of the International Conference of the Great Lakes Region, as well as the OECD due diligence guidance for responsible supply chains of minerals have been adopted to ensure the traceability of minerals and due diligence in supply chains, yet gaps persist due to fragmentation in implementation and the lack of coherence of these certification frameworks. The strengthening of institutions of governance complemented by national legislation which integrates certification and due diligence standards, is of critical importance to ensure compliance with standards and traceability of natural resources, including critical minerals. We still lack adequate identification measures throughout the complete value chain from source to the end product in order to break the illegal plundering of minerals and ensure state sovereignty over natural resources. For developing countries, capacity building, technical assistance, financial assistance, and technology transfer through multilateral and bilateral cooperation is of critical importance for strengthening institutions and ensuring coherence at local, regional, and international levels. Mr. President, South Africa is concerned about the illicit exploitation of natural resources in Africa, notably by transnational criminal networks that fuel instability and provide financing to armed groups. This remains a major concern, especially given the growing interest in the continent's vast reserves of critical minerals in light of global supply chain challenges and trade disputes. In addition, we would like to emphasize the importance of beneficiation and value addition of critical minerals within the African continent, ending illegal trade in minerals and enhancing regional cooperation to improve the African agency and benefit regarding these minerals globally. Mr. President, this Council itself has dealt with this thematic issue in various iterations and put in place listing criteria including linking to exploitation of natural resources and insecurity in various monitoring mechanisms of its respective sanctions regimes. Therefore, continued attention and expanding the scope of the Council's engagement on this matter would prove advantageous to address the illegal exploitation of natural resources and their role in fueling conflicts and instability. In conclusion, in this respect, the implementation of the decisions of the Security Council needs to be strengthened. Illicit financial flow traceability, the proliferation of arms should be halted, and private sector accountability should be assured. The Financial Action Task Force has demonstrated that it is possible to trace terrorism financing and money laundering. Similarly, illicit financial flows should be traced to halt the financing of armed groups. Most importantly, strong political will is needed for member states to effectively manage natural resources for the benefit of the people and also in order to comply with their international commitments fully in terms of international law, including international humanitarian and international human rights law.

I thank you.
I thank the representative of South Africa for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Brazil.

Mr. President, my delegation would like to thank you for convening this open debate on this particularly topical issue. At the outset, we'd like to make a key distinction. Natural resources are not in and of themselves the source of conflict, nor do they pose an intrinsic threat to international peace and security. Abundant natural resources can improve the quality of life of a population. Nonetheless, when they're poorly managed, they can exacerbate insecurity. On the contrary, management that's sustainable, transparent, and participatory, that's mainstreamed into sustainable development policies, can promote prosperity, social cohesion, and conflict prevention. The 1974 Charter for Economic Rights and Duties of States enshrines the full, permanent, and absolute sovereignty of each and every state over that state's wealth, natural resources, as well as its economic activities. It is therefore up to each and every state to determine the modalities for the use of these natural resources and to reap the benefits thereof. Any interpretation that could internationalize the management of these resources on the pretext of armed conflicts should be discarded. Having said that, growing demand for critical minerals required for the energy transition And the digital economy is intensifying certain resource use dynamics. In a number of situations, armed groups are funding their illicit activities through the illegal exploitation of said resources. This phenomenon is disproportionately affecting African countries and exposing vulnerable populations to human rights abuses. What it also does is serious damage to flora, fauna, and waterways. Conversely, Armed conflicts can result in environmental degradation, pollution, and biodiversity loss. As the Red Cross has reminded us, even if international humanitarian law protects the natural environment, military operations could— can do direct or indirect damage to environmental resources. We cannot let the energy transition, a transition which is so necessary, we cannot allow it to fuel new insecurity patterns. Mr. President, the Security Council should not become an environmental governance body. Within the confines of its mandate, the Security Council can address the security consequences of undue natural resource exploitation when such exploitation generates, fuels, or prolongs conflicts. Achieving peace isn't only about silencing the guns. We also need to tackle the structural causes of violence, frequently linked to socioeconomic development. Peace operations can bolster national regulatory oversight and police capacity. The Peacebuilding Commission can, for its part, support the training, the mobilization of resources, the coordination of actors, and the adoption of preventive approaches. Last but not least, Mr. President, strengthening national supervision should go hand in hand with multilateral and regional cooperation. The Kimberley Process, to which Brazil is a party, demonstrates how traceability and codes of conduct can turn natural resources into vectors of peace and development rather than a cause for conflict or a source of war financing. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Brazil. I now give the floor to the representative of Zimbabwe.

Thank you, Mr. President. Zimbabwe thanks the Democratic Republic of the Congo for convening this high-level open debate. We thank the Secretary-General and the Director-General of the World Trade Organization for their remarks. The central question is whether natural wealth advances peace or fuels conflict. The answer lies not in resources themselves, but in how they are governed, traded, and transformed. Mr. President, our consideration must begin with the Charter of the United Nations. Article 2 safeguards the sovereign authority of states over matters within domestic jurisdiction, without prejudice to enforcement measures under Chapter 7. General Assembly Resolution 1803 on permanent sovereignty over natural resources reinforces this principle, affirming the right of states and peoples to manage their natural wealth according to national interests and development priorities. Accordingly, primary responsibility for natural resource governance rests with sovereign states. International cooperation should complement that responsibility by supporting national ownership and strengthening institutions. Yet governance alone cannot overcome an international economic system that consigns developing countries to exporting raw commodities and importing higher-value manufactured goods. In this unequal exchange, resource-rich countries retain too little of the value generated from their natural resource. The peace dividend therefore lies not merely in extraction but in beneficiation, value addition, industrialization, employment, and improved livelihoods. Where this economic challenge intersects with conflict, the Security Council has a legitimate role. When illegal exploitation and trafficking of natural resources finance threats to international peace and security, Council engagement must remain focused, evidence-based, and consistent with the Charter. Natural resources in themselves do not cause conflict. Conflict is fueled when armed groups, terrorist organizations, and transnational criminal networks exploit and trade resources to finance violence. Effective international action must therefore target the enabling architecture— financiers, intermediaries, and illicit markets, supply chains, and arms networks. Curbing small arms and light weapons is essential since they enable illegal control of production areas and trade routes. Against this backdrop, Zimbabwe welcomes frameworks that promote responsible governance while respecting national ownership. The Kimberley Process demonstrates the value of nationally-led measures supported by international standards. At the continental level, Agenda 2063, the African Continental Free Trade Area, the African Commodities Strategy, the African Mining Vision, and the African Green Minerals Strategy promote value addition, diversification, strategic value chains, technological capability, and prudent stewardship. Their message is clear: Africa must not remain merely a source of raw materials for the industrialization of others. Building on these continental ambitions, Zimbabwe is advancing responsible mining, cleaner energy, and beneficiation across key mineral value chains. Our objective is to transform mineral wealth into domestic industry, employment, and inclusive prosperity, leaving no one and no place behind. Thank you, Mr. President. In conclusion, Mr. President, Zimbabwe reiterates 3 key points on this debate. First, international security discussions should focus on the actors in a conflict and not on inanimate materials such as raw natural resources. Second, permanent sovereignty over natural resources remains the foundational lens in which natural resources should be viewed and governed. And third, multilateral cooperation should focus on promoting value addition, beneficiation, and addressing the continued imbalanced global trade in commodities. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Zimbabwe for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Vietnam.

Mr. President, Vietnam sincerely thanks the Democratic Republic of Congo for convening this timely debate at a critical juncture when the nexus between natural resources and global peace, security, and sustainable development is more resonant than ever, particularly with the quest for energy transition and climate resilience. Yet we share concerns about fragmented rules, weak institutions, and unfair competition among states threatening to put developing countries at the lower tier of value chains and deprive them of legitimate interests. In this regard, allow us to offer 3 recommendations. First, the international community should adopt a comprehensive long-term approach corresponding to each country's circumstances, one that better integrates resource management into conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and post-conflict recovery. While ensuring that countries and communities can fully reap the benefits of the natural resources extracted from their homeland. Vietnam stands ready to actively engage with initiatives of the UN, the Secretariat-General, and regional and international organizations to spearhead those endeavors. Second, we firmly advocate stronger regional and international cooperation to construct harmonized, effective, and transparent rules and standards that fully respect the sovereignty and ownership of states over their natural resources. Any politicalizations and weaponizations of supply chains must be avoided for the benefit of all. Our region may offer useful experience. The ASEAN Principles on Sustainable Mineral Development, the ASEAN Minerals Cooperation Action Plan, the ASEAN Minerals Development Vision 2045, and the ASEAN Mineral Investment Forum have consolidated resource governance frameworks that generate mutual interest for our common community to thrive. Third, Vietnam's call for more technical assistance, knowledge sharing, and technological transfer for neighboring countries in sustainable mineral productions and processing. For its part, Vietnam is committed to responsible resource governance and will work closely with our partners so that natural resources become a genuine foundation for peace, security, and sustainable development. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Vietnam for their statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Stavros Lambrinidis, Head of the Delegation of the European Union to the United Nations.

I have the honors to deliver this statement on behalf of the EU and its member states. The candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Georgia, as well as Armenia, align themselves with this statement. Thank you, Mr. President, for convening this debate following the IREME meeting last week. There we all agreed that the illicit exploitation of natural resources continues to fuel armed conflicts, weaken state institutions, undermine sustainable development, particularly in conflict-affected regions, Sustainable peace in several conflict-torn regions of the world cannot be achieved without responsible resource governance. And for that, the participation of often neglected interlocutors— from women to indigenous peoples, from local communities to youth— is key. The European Union is strongly committed to preventing international trade in conflict minerals from intensifying or perpetuating conflicts and associated human rights abuses. The European Union's Conflict Minerals Regulation, in force since 2021, aims to break the link between minerals trade and armed conflict by promoting responsible sourcing of tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold. Regulation aligns with OECD due diligence guidance, and unlike voluntary frameworks, they use approaches legally binding Reaffirming, reinforcing accountability. The European Union further believes that producing countries should benefit more from their natural resources. This is the approach behind the EU's raw materials partnerships with partner countries. Under its Global Gateway initiative, the EU is a leading supporter of the Kivu-Kinshasa Green Corridor, a project launched by President Tshisekedi that, by combining conservation, clean hydropower and sustainable value chains expands legal livelihoods for local communities and reduces the space for the illicit exploitation of natural resources, fuelling armed conflict. The EU also remains firmly committed to advancing transparency, accountability and good governance across the extractive sector. As one of the leading donors of the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative, The EITI— the EU supports the implementation of the EITI standard, which is the leading global standard and benchmark for transparency in the sector. Last year, we further increased our support to strengthen capacity building and technical assistance for the implementation of the 2023 EITI standard in sub-Saharan Africa. Since 2016, the EU has also supported the World Bank's Multi-Donor Trust Fund Extractives Global Programmatic Support, which helps resource-rich low- and middle-income countries harness their mineral wealth for sustainable, inclusive socio-economic development. Chair, in the context of the Frank Bennett International Framework, the relevance of UN Security Council tools such as Panel of Experts, sanctions regimes, and the UNSC endorsement of the Kimberley Process cannot be overstated. Strengthening of these mechanisms and ensuring a greater coherence is essential. Let me in this regard highlight the recent strengthening of the European restrictive measures adopted on imports of Sudanese gold, and designed to curb sources of financing for the conflict and further increase pressure on those fuelling the war. The decision, I stress, includes targeted exceptions on goods intended for humanitarian purposes, public health emergencies and disaster response. Chair, in conclusion, critical raw materials, including those considered to be conflict minerals, are crucial factors of sustainable development. They should be drivers of prosperity and not sources of conflicts, human rights violations and other abuses. We should keep focus on this important issue, including by better applying the existing international framework. By supporting responsible business conduct, and by putting the rights of local producers in the center of our attention, the EU reaffirms its commitment to support producing countries in their efforts. And thank you again for the initiative you've taken.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Lambrinidis for that statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Cuba.

Thank you, President.

President.

We welcome the presence this morning in the chamber of Her Excellency Thérèse Karimbaya Wagner, Minister for Foreign Affairs of the DRC. People— the peoples of Africa, as well as Latin America and Asia, have been victims over decades of the looting of their natural resources as a result of colonialist practices by the major powers. Exploitation of these countries' resources by foreign powers and the negation of their rights to use their own resources are one of the major causes of the deep inequalities that continue to characterize the current international order and continue to hamper efforts to achieve development and peace throughout the world. The resolution of the General Assembly recognizes the rights that states have to use their own resources and to use their resources to achieve development. The exploitation of natural resources can lead to peace when these rights are fully respected, particularly the sovereign rights of states and the importance of peacefully settling disputes and refraining from interfering in states' sovereignty and their domestic affairs. These are fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter and international law. In addition, unilateral coercive measures are instruments of political pressure that violate international law and the U.N. Charter, and which have a serious impact on people's human rights and countries' ability to achieve development. President, for almost 70 years, Cuba has been a victim of the embargo imposed upon it by the United States government. Its extraterritorial application tries— aims to prevent Cuba from using its natural resources itself, and it also affects companies, banks, and other economic operators because they are all subject to threats from participating— as a result of participating in legitimate economic activities. I thank you.

For the most For the Maldives, our natural resources base is not minerals. It is the ocean. Tourism is the single largest contributor to the Maldives' GDP. Merci beaucoup.

By way of conclusion, Burundi would like to reaffirm its conviction that mining and environmental The natural riches on our continent must serve our people. They must not serve war. Thank you. Thank you, Madam President. Madam President, on behalf of Belgium, I'd like to applaud the work you've done as part of your presidency of the Security Council in July. Through its 2005 resolution, the Council reaffirmed its determination to take measures against the illegal exploitation and trafficking in natural resources. Belgium also supports efforts aiming to broaden the definition of a conflict diamond, and this within the framework of the Kimberley Process. Fourth, the Council should strengthen and act decisively on the basis of conclusions drawn by panels and groups of experts by holding accountable those who benefit from the illicit exploitation of natural resources. Blocking subsidiary bodies means that the Security Council has trouble exercising its responsibility in this area. Next, minerals extraction is accelerating not just on land but also at sea. Peaceful governance must also extend to the world's oceans. Belgium is actively contributing to strengthening international law and governance anchored We are also well represented in laws applicable to the sea. We are a party to the UNCLOS Convention. We're currently a member of the IMO Board, and we are a candidate for hosting the BBNJ Secretariat. Madam President, by way of conclusion, transparent, equitable, and responsible governance of natural resources resources is not simply an environmental nor an economic imperative. Madam President, Nigeria expresses its appreciation to the Democratic Republic of Congo and Your Excellency for convening this debate. In our Niger Delta area, control over oil revenue and years of crude theft financed militancy. until Nigeria's amnesty program and the Nigeria Extractive Industry Transparency Initiative began to change the trajectory. Indeed, it was revenue transparency and not enforcement alone that shifted the dynamic. It is sad that the same choice between resource-finance conflict and resource-finance development continues to play out wherever mineral wealth is contested. In the Lake Chad Basin and the Gulf of Guinea. The exploitation and theft of natural resources sustains networks that the Council already sanctions for arms trafficking and terrorism. Yet the Council's response has remained fragmented and country-specific, and no common framework yet treats resource governance and traceability as instruments of conflict prevention in their own right. First, the Council should extend the systematic tracing of natural resource financing across sanctions committees and the Panel of Experts so that resource revenue becomes a standard line of inquiry rather than an exception pursued on case-by-case basis. Second, the Council should back the regional bodies managing resource-linked conflict on the ground, including the Lake Chad Basin Commission and the Gulf of Guinea Commission, with predictable funding and capacity-building initiatives rather than ad hoc appeals, and draw on their assessment and experiences when designing sanctions and mandates. And third, the Council should ensure that extractive sector transparency, including beneficial ownership disclosure measures feeds directly into the Council's own conflict analysis so that a visible dividend for producing communities becomes the measure of success. To conclude, Nigeria views today's debate as a starting point. We look forward to working with the Council, the African Union, and our regional partners to see our recommendations and the ones made by other delegations carried into Council practice and returning to this chamber to assess the progress made. That, for resource-producing states including Nigeria, is the measure by which this debate should ultimately be judged. I thank you.

Transparent, accountable, and inclusive management addresses the root causes conflict, prevents relapse, and ensures that resource wealth benefits all. Strengthening institutions and promoting equitable management of natural resources are key to breaking the cycle of conflict Second, regional and international cooperation is indispensable for strengthening natural resource governance. 3.

Which was drafted to curb the illegal exploitation of natural resources. Madam President, the tragedy of blood diamonds taught the world a painful lesson. When the value of a mineral exceeds the value of human life, peace becomes the first casualty. The United Republic of Tanzania believes this lesson must become the foundation of a lasting global response to resource-driven conflict, and we commend the Democratic Republic of Congo for bringing this matter to the attention of this country— this Council this month of July. In the 1990s and early 2000s, the illicit trade in diamonds fueled devastating civil wars in Sierra Leone, Angola, and Liberia. Armed groups exchanged diamonds for weapons, prolonging violence that claimed hundreds of thousands of lives and displaced millions. Through Security Council action and the Kimberley Process Certification Scheme, the international community demonstrated the value of coordinated global governance in reducing the trade in conflict diamonds. It became evident that it is possible and something very doable. Yet the challenge has evolved with the critical and strategic minerals today. Today, the illicit exploitation of gold, tin, tantalum, tungsten, and other high-risk minerals continues to finance armed groups in several conflict-affected regions, threatening international peace and security. The Security Council has long recognized this nexus. The question before us is not whether we can act— we already have. It is whether we will apply the lessons of the blood diamonds to today's challenges by strengthening the global governance of minerals from conflict-affected and high-risk areas. Tanzania firmly believes that mineral wealth should finance development, not destruction. As a resource-rich nation, we have strengthened oversight of our mining sector through regulatory reforms, digital mineral trade monitoring, improved revenue collection, and greater transparency. These measures have increased public revenues while strengthening accountability. Our experience demonstrates that strong national institutions are the first line of defense against illicit resource exploitation. However, national efforts alone are insufficient. Illicit mineral supply chains cross borders and demand coordinated international action. Tanzania therefore proposed 4 priorities. First, expand traceability to all high-risk minerals through interoperable certification schemes and digital technologies that verify origin and prevent illicit trade. Second, make transparency the global standard by strengthening disclosure of revenue, contracts, and beneficial ownership to enhance accountability and public trust. Third, promote responsible and equitable mineral value chains through greater investment in local processing, technology transfer, infrastructure, and skill development, ensuring producing countries share fairly in the benefit of their resources. And fourth and finally, strengthen Africa-led solutions solution and supporting existing frameworks such as the Protocol Against the Illegal Exploitation of Natural Resources under the International Conference on Great Lakes Region and the Dar es Salaam Declaration on Peace, Security, Stability and Development. Madam President, United Republic of Tanzania calls upon this Council to strengthen the global framework for the responsible governance of minerals from conflict-affected and high-risk areas, ensuring that natural resources advance peace, sustainable development, and human security. Let the value of our natural resources be measured not by the profits they generate, but by peace, stability, and dignity they deliver to the people and communities from which they are drawn. Thank you.

A very good afternoon, colleagues. Argentina commends the Democratic Republic of the Congo as President of the Security Council for the month of July, and we would like to thank them for organizing this timely open debate. Madam President, the Security Council has already addressed the relation between the illicit exploitation of natural resources and the financing of conflicts. Argentina believes that the Council's work should be limited to those situations that genuinely constitute a threat to international peace and security. We think that we should avoid the promotion of global regulatory frameworks on natural resources that are subject to the permanent sovereignty of states. This is a principle that is enshrined in Resolution 1803 of the General Assembly. We recall that the use of natural resources should not be carried out and the exploitation should not be carried out in territories that are in dispute, particularly when the General Assembly has urged the parties to refrain from taking unilateral decisions on the matter while the dispute remains. An automatic link between environmental challenges and threats to international peace and security could lead to undesirable policies and institutional consequences. Although environmental degradation can indeed exacerbate tensions or conflicts in certain contexts, the response should not be to look at security the issue. In this regard and in a constructive way as a potential result of this debate, my delegation believes it would be useful to begin by looking at the volume and kinds of natural resources affected by conflicts. This exercise would make it possible to pinpoint with greater precision where the Council's work is necessary and should be prioritized, avoiding general responses for very different realities. Argentina also observes the initiatives for establishing global approaches on natural resources. The experience of the SG's Panel on Critical Minerals and the task force should not be converted into a precedent to move towards regulatory frameworks of a universal scope without a clear intergovernmental mandate and without due respect for the remits of the relevant bodies. Many developing countries have established their own institutional and legal frameworks for the responsible management and exploitation of their resources. The protection of the environment and the management of natural resources are legitimate urgent goals. However, this should be addressed in specialized fora in line with their respective mandates through international cooperation and with full respect for state sovereignty. As well as state circumstances, priorities, and national policies. Madam President, enormous importance today is attributed to critical minerals. This requires a broad, balanced approach. The need to diversify supply chains and to broaden production has significantly increased demand for these resources. While the main consumers are mainly located in developed countries, a substantial part of the reserves and productive potential is to be found in developing countries. In spite of this, Argentina wishes to underscore that the production of critical minerals is not by definition associated with conflict situations. For instance, Argentina possesses significant reserves of critical minerals. In this regard, the regime of incentives for major investments has been adopted, which aims to provide predictability and legal certainty for strategic projects and to ensure that benefits contribute to the country's social and economic development. Investment should go hand in hand with technology transfer to the development of infrastructure, capacity building, and international cooperation adapted and tailored to the needs of each country. Only in this way can producing states add value value, strengthen their capacity for management, and make the most of the resources they have for the benefit of their people. In conclusion, combating crimes affecting the environment both nationally and transnationally should be carried out through international cooperation and strengthen national capacities without undermining the legal competences of every country nor their sovereignty to administer their own natural resources. Thank you very much.
